extracted.intended_audience: USPTO policymakers, examiners, supervisors, quality specialists, patent practitioners and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and proposed metrics for using statistical monitoring to detect and address inconsistent or unreasonable patent examination across USPTO examiners, art units, and technology centers. Focuses on which statistics to collect, how to compare them, and what indicators should trigger investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of consistent, reasonable examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should expect that multiple examiners examining the same application will identify art of comparable quality, cooperate with applicants to a similar degree, and interpret patent law in a similar manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline desideratum: examination should be both consistent across examiners/art units and reasonable in application of law. Variability that prevents applicants from reasonably predicting outcomes (e.g., allowance likelihood, degree of claim narrowing) is unacceptable and should prompt review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allowance rate as a key examiner/art-unit statistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate each examiner's and art unit's allowance rate (percentage of applications allowed) as a core statistic to evaluate consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare allowance rates across examiners/art units; a wide spread (e.g., 7% to 86% in an art unit) indicates inconsistent examination. The center of the distribution can be assessed against appeal results and quality specialist reviews to determine reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average office-action counts per patent/application
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the number of office actions issued per patent (and/or per abandonment) for each examiner/art unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High average numbers of office actions or sequential non-final office actions may indicate unreasonable rejections or poor initial examination quality. Use these counts to spot examiners/art units that deviate from peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average number of interviews per application
rubrics_metrics.description: Track how often examiners conduct interviews (average interviews per application) as an engagement metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant differences in interview prevalence between examiners/art units may reflect differing prosecution styles or engagement levels; include in comparative dashboards to evaluate cooperative engagement with applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction requirement prevalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the frequency with which an examiner or art unit issues restriction requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High or low prevalence relative to peers may indicate inconsistent application of restriction practice; include as part of multi-metric monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of particular programs or practices (e.g., interviews, AFCP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor an examiner's or art unit's use of specific programs/practices such as interviewing or the After-Final Consideration Program (AFCP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in usage rates of established programs can reveal variation in how examiners apply available procedures to advance prosecution; track program participation alongside outcome metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal-related statistics (prevalence, reopen frequency, PTAB outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect statistics about appeals: prevalence of appeal filings, frequency of prosecution being reopened during appeal, and PTAB / Pre-Appeal Brief Conference decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High prevalence of appeals or frequent reopening of prosecution during appeals may flag poor-quality rejections. PTAB reversals and Pre-Appeal outcomes should be included as indicators of potentially unreasonable examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution tightness and center-of-distribution assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the distribution of each statistic across examiners is tight (narrow) and evaluate the center of that distribution for reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A narrow distribution suggests consistent examination; the central tendency should be validated using appeal results and quality reviews to determine whether the 'typical' behavior is reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and investigation of statistical outliers
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify outlier examiners or art units on monitored statistics and initiate investigations or discussions rather than automatic sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outliers should trigger a fact-finding process: review lower-level data, discuss findings with the examiner and supervisor, and consider valid explanatory factors before taking action. Do not impose hardline responses solely because of outlier status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical indicators of unreasonable examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific statistical signals as likely indicators of unreasonable examination: reopening of prosecution during the appeal cycle, multiple sequential non-final office actions, and PTAB reversals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these signals as priority flags for review and deeper analysis; corroborate with case-level data and supervisory/quality-specialist review before concluding unreasonable practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide access to examination statistics to multiple Office levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure examiners, supervisors, quality specialists, and leadership have access to examiner- and art-unit-level statistics and comparative data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should see their own statistics and how they compare (at least within their art unit). Supervisors and quality specialists should review data at examiner, art-unit, and technology-center levels to identify variation and opportunities for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider application- and applicant-level variability when interpreting statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that legitimate differences (invention subject matter, drafting quality, applicant behavior, assignment bias) can affect statistics; adjust interpretation accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming raw differences imply misconduct. Where assignment bias or differing applicant behavior may explain variation, control for these factors in analysis or use investigations to surface contextual reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor investigation and dialogue over hardline remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: When statistical monitoring identifies anomalies, prefer initiating investigations and discussions with supervisors/examiners rather than imposing hard rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal explicitly recommends investigating and discussing outlier data, acknowledging valid underlying circumstances may exist. Use findings to inform training, supervisory action, or policy adjustments rather than immediate punitive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a statistical approach as an objective starting point
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt statistics as an objective, initial method to evaluate examination characteristics and identify potential inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics (allowance rates, office-action counts, interviews, appeals metrics, etc.) serve as an ideal starting point; subsequent assessment should combine these metrics with appeals/quality specialist reviews and case-level analysis.
